title: 3.5 Cell Transport
description: How substances move across the cell membrane: passive and active transport

questions.question: What is the main characteristic of passive transport?
options: It requires energy (ATP) to move substances
It moves substances against their concentration gradient
It does not require cellular energy and moves substances down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Passive transport moves substances from high to low concentration (down the concentration gradient) without requiring cellular energy (ATP).

questions.question: What is the main characteristic of active transport?
options: It moves substances down their concentration gradient
It requires energy (ATP) to move substances against their concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Active transport requires cellular energy (ATP) to move substances from low to high concentration (against the concentration gradient).

questions.question: What is diffusion?
options: The movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane
The movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration
The movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy
The movement of large molecules into a cell
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down the concentration gradient.

questions.question: What is osmosis?
options: The diffusion of any solute across a membrane
The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution
The movement of gases in the air
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of higher water concentration (dilute) to lower water concentration (concentrated).

questions.question: What is a hypotonic solution?
options: A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell
A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell
A solution with the same solute concentration as the cell
A solution that contains no solutes at all
questions.explanation: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration (higher water concentration) than the cell. Water enters the cell by osmosis.

questions.question: What is a hypertonic solution?
options: A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell
A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell
A solution with the same solute concentration as the cell
A solution that contains only water
questions.explanation: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration (lower water concentration) than the cell. Water leaves the cell by osmosis.

questions.question: What is an isotonic solution?
options: A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell
A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell
A solution with the same solute concentration as the cell
questions.explanation: An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cell. There is no net movement of water into or out of the cell.

questions.question: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
options: It becomes turgid as water enters the cell by osmosis
questions.explanation: In a hypotonic solution, water enters the plant cell by osmosis, causing it to swell and become turgid. The cell wall prevents bursting.

questions.question: What happens to an animal cell (e.g., red blood cell) placed in a hypotonic solution?
options: It swells and may burst (hemolysis) due to water entering by osmosis
questions.explanation: Animal cells lack a cell wall. In hypotonic solution, water enters by osmosis, causing the cell to swell and potentially burst (hemolysis in red blood cells).

questions.question: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: It undergoes plasmolysis — the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall as water leaves
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the plant cell by osmosis. The vacuole shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall — this is plasmolysis.

questions.question: What happens to an animal cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: It shrinks and crenates (becomes shriveled) as water leaves by osmosis
questions.explanation: In hypertonic solution, water leaves animal cells by osmosis, causing them to shrink and shrivel (crenation).

questions.question: What is turgor pressure?
options: The pressure exerted by the cell wall against the expanded cell membrane when a plant cell is turgid
The force that moves water up a plant stem
questions.explanation: Turgor pressure is the outward pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall when the cell is turgid (full of water). It provides structural support to plants.

questions.question: What is plasmolysis?
options: The bursting of a cell due to excess water
The shrinkage of the cell membrane away from the cell wall in a plant cell due to water loss
The uptake of minerals by active transport
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution; water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks, and the cell membrane detaches from the cell wall.

questions.question: What type of transport is required to move glucose into most cells against its concentration gradient?
questions.explanation: Glucose is often transported into cells against its concentration gradient via active transport, requiring ATP and carrier proteins.

questions.question: What is facilitated diffusion?
options: Diffusion that requires a protein carrier or channel but no cellular energy
Diffusion that only occurs in plants
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport where substances move down their concentration gradient through specific protein channels or carriers, without using ATP.

questions.question: Which of the following transport processes does NOT require energy?
options: Pumping of sodium ions out of the cell
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion is a passive process that does not require energy. Active transport, endocytosis, and ion pumping all require ATP.

questions.question: What is the role of carrier proteins in active transport?
options: They allow water to pass through
They bind to specific substances and use ATP to move them across the membrane against the concentration gradient
They provide structural support to the membrane
questions.explanation: Carrier proteins in active transport bind to specific molecules, change shape using energy from ATP, and transport the molecules across the membrane.

questions.question: Which solution would be used to rehydrate a wilted plant?
questions.explanation: A wilted plant has lost water. Placing it in a hypotonic solution (water) allows water to enter cells by osmosis, restoring turgidity.

questions.question: Why does salting food (e.g., fish or meat) preserve it?
options: Salt prevents bacteria from entering the food
Salt creates a hypertonic environment that causes bacteria to lose water and die through plasmolysis
Salt kills bacteria by providing them with too much energy
Salt dilutes the food so bacteria cannot grow
questions.explanation: Salt creates a hypertonic environment. Water leaves bacterial cells by osmosis, causing them to shrivel and die (plasmolysis), preserving the food.

questions.question: What happens to red blood cells when placed in an isotonic solution (e.g., 0.9% saline)?
options: They remain normal — no net movement of water
questions.explanation: In an isotonic solution, the solute concentration inside and outside the cell is equal, so there is no net movement of water, and the cells maintain their normal shape.

questions.question: What type of transport is involved when a cell engulfs a large particle by forming a vesicle?
questions.explanation: Endocytosis is an active transport process where the cell membrane invaginates to engulf large particles, forming a vesicle inside the cell.

questions.question: What is the term for the process where a cell expels large molecules by fusing a vesicle with the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Exocytosis is the active transport process where vesicles fuse with the cell membrane to release their contents outside the cell.

questions.question: How does oxygen move from the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a small non-polar molecule that moves by simple diffusion from a high concentration (alveoli) to a low concentration (blood), down its concentration gradient.

questions.question: What is the main difference between simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion?
options: Simple diffusion requires ATP; facilitated diffusion does not
Simple diffusion moves substances through the lipid bilayer directly; facilitated diffusion uses protein channels or carriers
Facilitated diffusion requires ATP; simple diffusion does not
Simple diffusion only works for water
questions.explanation: In simple diffusion, substances pass directly through the lipid bilayer. In facilitated diffusion, substances pass through specific protein channels or carrier proteins.

questions.question: What is the effect of placing a freshwater protozoan (e.g., Paramecium) in pond water?
options: It swells because water enters by osmosis; it must use a contractile vacuole to pump out excess water
questions.explanation: Pond water is hypotonic to Paramecium. Water constantly enters by osmosis. The contractile vacuole collects and pumps out excess water to prevent bursting.

questions.question: Which of the following requires ATP?
options: Movement of $CO_2$ out of a cell
Movement of $Na^+$ ions out of a cell against the concentration gradient
questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump actively transports $Na^+$ out of the cell against its concentration gradient, requiring ATP. $O_2$, $CO_2$, and water move by passive processes.

questions.question: What happens to the turgidity of a plant when it is watered after being dry?
options: It increases — cells absorb water and become turgid again
questions.explanation: When watered, water enters plant cells by osmosis, the vacuoles fill, turgor pressure increases, and the plant becomes firm (turgid) again.

questions.question: What would happen to a plant if it is watered with a concentrated salt solution?
options: It would grow faster due to added minerals
It would wilt because the soil becomes hypertonic, causing water to leave the roots by osmosis
questions.explanation: Concentrated salt solution creates a hypertonic environment. Water moves out of root cells by osmosis, causing the plant to wilt (plasmolysis).

questions.question: What is the selectively permeable property of the cell membrane?
options: It allows all substances to pass freely
It blocks all substances from entering
It allows some substances to pass through while restricting others
It only allows water to pass through
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is selectively permeable (semi-permeable) — it allows certain substances to pass through while preventing others from crossing.

questions.question: Which factor increases the rate of diffusion?
questions.explanation: A steeper concentration gradient increases the rate of diffusion. Higher temperature and larger surface area also increase diffusion rates.
